idiom_name: hand-written cursor struct (init/next protocol), GLib iterators as the library precedent
implementation_notes: C has no iteration protocol, so the classic roles are hand-written: an opaque cursor struct owns the traversal state and the aggregate hands out an initialized cursor instead of exposing its storage. GLib is the closest thing to a library realization - GHashTableIter is a stack-allocated struct initialized with g_hash_table_iter_init() and advanced with g_hash_table_iter_next(), while GSequenceIter represents a position between two elements with explicit begin/end iterators, exactly like an STL iterator; plain GList/GQueue code instead walks node pointers directly (for-loop over ->next or g_list_foreach, which is internal iteration). Hand-written cursors stay the right choice where a GLib dependency is unacceptable or the layout is custom (arenas, intrusive lists), and for a contiguous array a plain index loop remains simpler than any cursor.
pitfalls: The cursor stores a raw pointer into the aggregate: any realloc/append that moves the backing array turns a live cursor into a dangling pointer, and GLib documents the same hazard (modifying a GHashTable invalidates its iterator).
C offers no ownership or lifetime guarantees, so the aggregate must outlive every iterator handed out of it - there is no borrow checker and no exception to unwind the cursor.
Every project invents its own convention (bool + out-param, NULL sentinel, negative return), so cursors from different modules do not compose; pick one protocol per codebase and document it.
